blocks.text: At the Paris Sorbonne’s Galerie Soufflot, steps from the Panthéon, French photographer Catherine Balet stages an audacious replay of photography’s greatest hits — all of it unfolding during the 7th edition of the Photo Days festival.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Catherine Balet.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Nan Goldin, Nan and Brian in Bed, NYC, 1983, 2014. Courtesy Bigaignon

blocks.text: A graduate of the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts de Paris, Balet came to photography as a painter, making the switch in the early 2000s. Her work moves in series: “Identity,” then “Strangers in the Light,” both published by Steidl, map out a practice fed by sociology, painting, and a restless hunger for what images burn into collective memory.

blocks.alt: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Eadweard Muybridge, Homme montant des escaliers, 1887, 2014. Courtesy Bigaignon
blocks.caption: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Claude Cahun, Que me veux-tu ?, 1928, 2014. Courtesy Bigaignon

blocks.text: The spark came at the Rencontres d’Arles in the summer of 2013, where Balet watched the photographers on the walls and decided she wanted to play. Her accomplice: Ricardo Martinez Paz, a longtime friend — a former actor trained at the Conservatorio Nacional de Buenos Aires, a Parisian stylist since 1977, and a septuagenarian of incandescent presence. He became her muse. “It’s his personality, luminous and complex, that inspired this whole series,” she told Phototrend in 2021.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Eadweard Muybridge, Homme montant des escaliers, 1887, 2014. Courtesy Bigaignon

blocks.text: In front of the lens, Ricardo steps into the shoes — literally golden — of the models. He climbs a staircase, naked, in the stuttering frames of Eadweard Muybridge’s 1887 motion study. He becomes Kiki de Montparnasse, face tilted beside an African mask, channeling Man Ray’s most iconic shot. He doubles as both figures in Claude Cahun’s uncanny late-1920s self-portrait. He hauls a boulder through the dreamscape of Grete Stern. He kisses in the street for Doisneau. And for Nan Goldin, he plays both roles at once — sprawled on the bed, then turned away, cigarette in hand, the lover Brian.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Robert Doisneau, Le Baiser de l’hôtel de ville, 1950, 2014. Courtesy Bigaignon

blocks.text: The approach is unorthodox, but it earns its intellectual keep twice over: as a sincere homage to the masters, and as an act of resurrection, restoring flesh and weight to the figures who inhabit these images-turned-icons. Each reconstruction holds true to the original — its light, its grain, its posture — with the precision of a watchmaker who happens to be in love. The result walks a tightrope between historical rigor, tender parody, and something close to grace.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Sorbonne Artgallery © Catherine Balet, in collaboration with Ricardo Martinez Paz, Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes, Homage to Grete Stern, Sueño nº15, 1949, 2019. Courtesy Bigaignon

blocks.text: For anyone who missed this work in its earlier showings, or at Galerie Bigaignon — which represents the artist in Paris and first exhibited the series in 2016 — this new hang is the perfect way in to a body of work as erudite as it is exhilarating.

“Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes” by Catherine Balet is on view at the Sorbonne Artgallery (Galerie Soufflot), 12 place du Panthéon, Paris 5th arrondissement, November 3–30, 2026. Free admission with a downloadable pass, Monday through Saturday, 10am–6pm.
